en: Created for a particular purpose only, not planned in advance
hook: AD HOC: Latin for 'for this' — for this one purpose only.
story: Ad hoc. Made for one particular purpose only, not planned in advance. One monsoon night, water rushed into the ground floor of a small-town hospital. There was no plan for this, so nurses, cleaners and patients' relatives formed an ad hoc team on the spot, passing beds and medicine boxes up the stairs, hand to hand. By morning the job was done, and the team simply melted away. Ad hoc is Latin for "for this": for this one job only. So, what do you call a team put together on the spot for a single task? ... Ad hoc.

gre.s: Rather than developing a coherent policy, the ministry responded to each crisis in a purely ____ fashion, devising quick fixes that were abandoned once the emergency passed.
gre.clue: Rather than developing a coherent policy

example: Without a written schedule, the volunteers at the book fair relied on ad hoc arrangements, deciding each morning who would staff which stall.

en: To permit; also, to admit or concede that something is true
hook: GRE trick: ALLOW can mean ADMIT — 'he allowed that he was wrong.'
story: Allow. To permit, and also to admit that something is true. Jake and his grandfather argued all through dinner about whose generation had it harder. Grandfather spoke of walking to school through knee-deep mud; Jake spoke of city traffic. At last the old man [chuckle] put down his tea. "I will allow that your traffic is worse than my mud." Jake [laugh] grinned and allowed that the mud sounded terrible too. When you allow a point into the argument, you admit it is true. So, what verb means to admit that the other side has a point? ... Allow.

gre.s: Even her harshest critics would ____ that her research was meticulous, though they continued to dispute the conclusions she drew from it.
gre.clue: though they continued to dispute the conclusions

example: The referee later allowed that the goal might have been offside, though he insisted he had no clear view at the time.

en: Suitable or proper for the situation (adj.); to take something for one's own use, often without permission (verb)
hook: Two pronunciations: ap-PRO-pree-it means SUITABLE; ap-PRO-pree-ate means to TAKE as your PROPERTY.
story: Appropriate. As an adjective, suitable for the situation. As a verb, to take something for your own use, often without permission. Ryan spent a month painting a poster for his university's spring festival. A week later, a senior student hung it in the hall with his own name at the bottom. Ryan felt his face burn. The senior had appropriated his work, and it was hardly appropriate behaviour. Inside appropriate hides the root of property, meaning your own: to appropriate is to make something your property. So, what verb means to take someone else's work as your own? ... Appropriate.

gre.s: Critics accused the fashion house of choosing to ____ traditional Jamdani motifs for its new collection without ever crediting the weavers who had developed them over centuries.
gre.clue: without ever crediting the weavers

example: During the war, the army appropriated several private villas in the hills and turned them into field hospitals.

en: Respected and impressive; majestic
hook: GRE trick: au-GUST, like Emperor AUGUSTUS, majestic.
story: August. Respected and impressive; majestic. On convocation day, an eighty-year-old professor walked onto the stage in his black gown, white-haired and perfectly upright. Two thousand graduates rose to their feet, and even the noisy photographers fell silent. Emily felt a shiver of pride just to be in that august hall, before such an august figure. Think of Augustus, the Roman emperor whose very title meant the revered one; an august person carries that same grandeur. So, what word describes a presence so dignified that a whole hall stands in silence? ... August.

gre.s: The young scholar felt intimidated in the ____ company of Nobel laureates and former heads of state, and barely dared to speak during the entire dinner.
gre.clue: Nobel laureates and former heads of state

example: The journal, founded in 1887, is one of the most august publications in the field, and acceptance there can make a young chemist's career.

en: Shamefully dishonorable and selfish, lacking any moral decency
hook: GRE trick: BASE means LOW morally, like the bottom of a building.
story: Base. Shamefully dishonourable and selfish, without moral decency. During a flood in a river town, one shopkeeper locked away his rice and sold it to hungry families at three times the normal price. When a relief volunteer begged him to be fair, he only raised the price again. The villagers were disgusted. Of all the things they saw that year, his greed was the most base. Picture the lowest floor of a building: a base act sinks to the very bottom of human behaviour. So, what word describes cheating desperate people for profit? ... Base.

gre.s: Investigators concluded that the official had acted from the most ____ motives, since he had accepted bribes to approve a dam he knew was unsafe.
gre.clue: accepted bribes to approve a dam he knew was unsafe

example: Spreading false rumors about a rival candidate's family was a base tactic, and even his own supporters were ashamed of it.

en: To publicly support or fight for a cause
hook: GRE trick: to CHAMPION a cause means to fight FOR it.
story: Champion. To publicly support or fight for a cause. When the council planned to fill in an old pond in a quiet town to build a market, a retired schoolteacher named Margaret refused to stay quiet. She wrote to newspapers, gathered her former students, and spoke at every public meeting. When the plan was finally dropped, Margaret [laugh] hugged the children who had marched with her. She had championed the pond. The trick: a sports champion wins for himself, but when you champion a cause, you fight for something beyond yourself. So, what verb means to stand up publicly for a cause? ... Champion.

gre.s: Though she was initially skeptical of renewable energy, the senator went on to ____ it more vigorously than any of her colleagues, sponsoring dozens of bills to expand solar power.
gre.clue: sponsoring dozens of bills to expand solar power

example: The young librarian championed a reading program for street children in Kamalapur, persuading local businesses to donate books and snacks.

en: Belonging to the same period as another; also, of the present day
hook: CON-TEMPORARY: with (con) the same time (tempus).
story: Contemporary. Belonging to the same period as someone else; also, of the present day. In nineteen thirty, the Indian poet Tagore sat with Albert Einstein near Berlin and talked about truth and reality. Hannah read about it for her history class and was amazed. The poet she grew up reciting and the scientist from her physics book were contemporaries, alive at the same time. Today the word can also mean modern, as in contemporary art. Con means with, and tempus means time: with the same time. So, what word describes two people who lived in the same era? ... Contemporary.

gre.s: Historians prefer ____ accounts of the battle, written by eyewitnesses, to the romanticized versions that poets composed a full century later.
gre.clue: written by eyewitnesses

example: Shakespeare and Cervantes were contemporary writers, and the two men died within days of each other in the spring of 1616.

en: Peacefully satisfied
hook: CON-TENT (stress on TENT): happy in your little tent.
story: Content. Peacefully satisfied. Tom rows a wooden boat on a wide river. Each evening he sits outside his tin-roofed house with a cup of sweet tea, [sigh] watching the sky turn orange over the water. When a visitor from the city asked whether he wanted more from life, Tom smiled, [chuckle] and shook his head. "I have enough." He was truly content. Content is the root of contentment; do not mix it up with the content of a book, which is what the book contains. So, what word describes someone peacefully satisfied with what they have? ... Content.

gre.s: Unlike her restless siblings, who constantly chased new ventures, she was ____ with the quiet life of a village schoolteacher and never sought promotion.
gre.clue: Unlike her restless siblings, who constantly chased new ventures

example: After years of chasing promotions in Dhaka, Kamal was finally content to run a small guesthouse among the tea gardens of Srimangal.

en: Following accepted customs and standards; traditional
hook: CONVENTIONAL: what everyone agreed on at the CONVENTION.
story: Conventional. Following accepted customs and standards; traditional. At a family dinner, Ethan's parents discussed his future: doctor, engineer, or a government job. Safe, respected, conventional. Then Ethan quietly said he wanted to photograph tigers in the mangrove forests. The table went silent, and his mother slowly put down her spoon. A convention is a meeting where people come to an agreement, so the conventional path is the one everyone has already agreed on. So, what word describes the safe, traditional path that everyone expects you to take? ... Conventional.

gre.s: Defying ____ wisdom, which held that the disease was inherited, the researcher argued that it was caused by an environmental toxin.
gre.clue: which held that the disease was inherited

example: The architect rejected the conventional glass tower and designed an office block wrapped in screens of living bamboo.

en: To regard as unimportant or untrustworthy; to disregard
hook: GRE trick: DISCOUNT means to ignore, not just lower the price.
story: Discount. To regard something as unimportant or untrustworthy, and set it aside. When a neighbour told Lily's grandmother that bitter gourd juice could replace her insulin, Lily felt a flash of worry. But the doctor gently discounted the advice and kept her grandmother on her medicine. After that, Lily learned to discount the miracle cures forwarded in family chats. The trick: in a shop, a discount cuts the price; in an argument, discounting a claim cuts its value to almost nothing. So, what verb means to dismiss a claim as not worth trusting? ... Discount.

gre.s: Scientists were quick to ____ the anonymous report, since its author offered no data and had a long history of fabricating results.
gre.clue: had a long history of fabricating results

example: Coach Habib discounted the injury rumors and named his striker in the starting eleven for the final.

en: Consisting of or based on real documents or facts
hook: DOCUMENTARY: backed by DOCUMENTS.
story: Documentary. Based on real documents and records. For years, Nathan's family argued over who owned a small plot of land in the countryside. Every uncle had a story, but stories proved nothing. Then Nathan opened his great-grandfather's old tin trunk and found the deed, the paper brown and brittle, the seal still clear. His aunt [gasp] pressed a hand to her mouth. At last there was documentary proof. The word has document right inside it: documentary evidence is evidence written down on paper. So, what kind of evidence rests on written records rather than memory? ... Documentary.

gre.s: The historian's claims rest on solid ____ evidence, including letters, ledgers, and court records from the period.
gre.clue: including letters, ledgers, and court records

example: No documentary proof of the land sale survived the fire, so the court had to rely on the testimony of elderly villagers.

en: Using money, effort or words sparingly and without waste
hook: GRE trick: ECONOMY of words means using no more words than needed.
story: Economy. Using money, effort or words carefully, without waste. Olivia's mother runs a family of five on one small salary. She buys vegetables in season, measures cooking oil by the spoon, and turns last night's leftovers into breakfast. Nothing is ever wasted. Years later, Olivia writes her essays the same way, with an economy of words that her teacher praises. Think of economy class on a plane: no extra space, nothing wasted. So, what word means careful use of money, effort or words, with nothing wasted? ... Economy.

gre.s: Her prose is admired for its remarkable ____: she never uses three words where one will do, and every sentence seems to earn its place.
gre.clue: she never uses three words where one will do

example: With remarkable economy of movement, the old carpenter smoothed the plank in a few strokes while his apprentice watched in silence.

en: Basic; relating to the simplest beginning stages
hook: ELEMENTARY: the basic ELEMENTS.
story: Elementary. Basic; belonging to the simplest beginning stages. On the first day of his GRE quant course, Kevin felt almost insulted. The teacher started with fractions, percentages and the area of a triangle, things he had learned in class six. Then his first practice test came back, and he had missed four elementary questions. [sigh] He stopped complaining and started practising. Elementary comes from element, the basic building block of everything. So, what word describes the simplest, most basic ideas a subject begins with? ... Elementary.

gre.s: Although the textbook advertises itself as an advanced treatment of the subject, its exercises are so ____ that a first-year student could finish them in an afternoon.
gre.clue: a first-year student could finish them in an afternoon

example: The first experiment in the chemistry lab was elementary, just timing how quickly salt dissolves in warm and cold water.

en: Feeling owed special treatment that one has not earned
bn: নিজেকে বিশেষ সুবিধার যোগ্য মনে করে এমন; অধিকারবোধসম্পন্ন
hook: ENTITLED: acts like he holds a royal TITLE.
story: Entitled. Feeling owed special treatment you have not earned. At the university canteen, students waited in a long line for lunch. A boy in designer sunglasses walked straight to the front and said, "Do you know who my father is?" The cashier calmly pointed to the back of the line, and a few students quietly cheered. He was entitled, acting as if rules were only for other people. Picture him wearing an invisible royal title: an entitled person behaves like a lord without ever earning the crown. So, what word describes someone who expects privileges they never earned? ... Entitled.

gre.s: The coach was frustrated by the star player's ____ attitude, as he expected special privileges while skipping the practices everyone else attended.
gre.clue: expected special privileges

example: The entitled customer at the Gulshan restaurant demanded a free dessert simply because he had waited five minutes for his table.

en: Natural ease or skill in doing something
hook: GRE trick: FACILITY means ease — she has a facility for languages.
story: Facility. A natural ease or skill in doing something. Grace's little brother has never had a single music lesson, yet he can hear a song once on the radio and play it on the harmonium straight away. His fingers find the notes as if they already knew them. When he finishes, the whole family [laugh] claps and cheers. Everyone notices his facility with melody. Facility shares its Latin root with facile and facilitate, all from the word for easy, so a facility is a skill that comes easily. So, what word means a natural ease at doing something? ... Facility.

gre.s: Despite her obvious ____ with languages, which allowed her to pick up conversational Italian in a matter of weeks, she struggled for years with basic arithmetic.
gre.clue: pick up conversational Italian in a matter of weeks

example: Rafsan's facility with numbers made him the person everyone called whenever the family's tax forms had to be filled in.

en: Open, honest, and direct
hook: FRANK: Frank always tells it straight.
story: Frank. Open, honest and direct. Daniel nervously handed his first short story to his mentor, hoping for praise. She read it, put down her tea, and said, "The opening is dull, and the ending is borrowed. But the third page is brilliant. Build from there." It stung, yet Daniel walked home grateful. She had been frank with him, and her frank words helped more than any polite ones. The trick: the old French word franc meant free, so frank speech is free of disguise. So, what word describes feedback that is open, honest and direct? ... Frank.

gre.s: Rather than offering the vague reassurances his patients expected, the doctor was always ____, telling them plainly what their prognosis was even when the news was grim.
gre.clue: telling them plainly what their prognosis was

example: In a frank interview, the retired captain admitted that his team had been badly unprepared for the tour of Australia.

en: Extremely small; precise and detailed (pronounced my-NOOT)
hook: MINUTE (my-NOOT): as tiny as a MINI thing.
story: Minute. Extremely small; also, precise and detailed. In a weaving village near the city, Sophie watched an old weaver lift threads one by one, working a minute flower into the cloth. Each petal was smaller than a grain of rice. One sari can take him months of such minute work, and Sophie could hardly breathe as she watched. Unlike the minute on a clock, this minute is about size, and it shares its root with diminish and minuscule, both about smallness. So, what word describes detail so tiny you must lean close to see it? ... Minute.

gre.s: Although the changes to the manuscript appeared ____, they altered the meaning of several key passages in ways that scholars still debate.
gre.clue: they altered the meaning of several key passages

example: Engineers found that a minute crack in a turbine blade, thinner than a hair, had caused the entire engine to fail.

en: Having high moral qualities; aristocratic
hook: NOBLE: like a NOBEL Prize-worthy character.
story: Noble. Having high moral qualities; also, aristocratic. A rickshaw puller in the city found a bag under his seat holding a small fortune. He had rent to pay and a daughter who needed school fees. Still, he spent the whole day searching until he found the owner, returned every note, and refused a reward. People who read the story felt their throats tighten. It was noble, nobler than any title. The trick: noble is the opposite of base; base sinks low, noble rises high. So, what word describes an act of high moral character, like returning money you badly need? ... Noble.

gre.s: Although she could easily have kept the reward for herself, she made the ____ choice to donate it to the families of the miners who had died.
gre.clue: Although she could easily have kept the reward for herself

example: Giving up his own scholarship so that his younger sister could study abroad was a noble sacrifice, though Nayeem never spoke of it.

en: Easily shaped or molded; flexible and adaptable
hook: GRE trick: PLASTIC means moldable, like clay — not just the material.
story: Plastic. Easily shaped or moulded; flexible and adaptable. Rachel's little son moved from a small town to the big city at four. Within months he was chattering in a new accent, picking up words from cousins and cartoons. Rachel worried, but her neighbour, a doctor, smiled and said, "A child's brain is plastic. It reshapes itself as it learns." The word comes from a Greek verb meaning to mould, which is also how the material plastic got its name. Think of soft clay in a potter's hands. So, what word describes something that can be easily shaped and reshaped? ... Plastic.

gre.s: Contrary to the old belief that the adult brain is fixed, researchers now regard it as remarkably ____, capable of forming new connections throughout life.
gre.clue: capable of forming new connections throughout life

example: Young children's accents are remarkably plastic, so a girl who moves from Sylhet to London at five may soon sound entirely British.

en: To prepare someone or something for action
hook: GRE trick: to PRIME is to PREPARE, like priming a wall before painting.
story: Prime. To prepare someone or something for action. In the last week before Megan's GRE, her tutor taught her nothing new. Instead, every morning at nine, the exact hour of her real test, he handed her a timed practice set, so her mind would wake up sharp at that time. He was priming her for the big day. It is just like a house painter priming a wall with a base coat before the real colour goes on. So, what verb means to get someone ready for action? ... Prime.

gre.s: Before the negotiations began, the lawyer took care to ____ her client, rehearsing every likely question so that nothing would catch him off guard.
gre.clue: rehearsing every likely question so that nothing would catch him off guard

example: Before the debate, the team captain primed each speaker with the opposing side's strongest arguments and the best replies to them.

en: Favoring drastic change; relating to the fundamental nature of something
hook: RADICAL: down to the ROOT (radix).
story: Radical. Favouring drastic change; also, relating to the very roots of something. For years, a riverside village fought floods with small fixes: sandbags, higher plinths, new drains. Every monsoon, the water won. Then a young engineer named Marcus made a radical proposal: build homes on floating platforms that rise with the water. The elders [gasp] stared at him in disbelief. Radical comes from the Latin radix, meaning root, so radical change goes all the way down to the roots. So, what word describes change that is drastic and fundamental? ... Radical.

gre.s: Rather than tinkering with the existing curriculum, the new principal proposed a ____ overhaul that would reshape every course from the ground up.
gre.clue: reshape every course from the ground up

example: Moving the whole newsroom from print to online publishing in a single year was a radical step for the century-old newspaper.

en: To consider something carefully; to show or express something
hook: REFLECT: like a mirror, turning thoughts back on yourself.
story: Reflect. To think carefully about something; also, to show or express it. After failing her first GRE practice test, Jessica looked at the score, [sigh] and did not rush into another one. She sat by her hostel window with the report and reflected. Which questions had she rushed? Which words had she only guessed? Three months later, her final score reflected all that patient work. Think of a mirror: it reflects your face, and when you reflect, you turn your thoughts back on yourself. So, what verb means to think deeply, or to show something clearly? ... Reflect.

gre.s: The novel's bleak tone may ____ the author's own despair during the war years, a period she described in her letters as the darkest of her life.
gre.clue: a period she described in her letters as the darkest of her life

example: Rising rents in Dhanmondi reflect the growing demand for apartments near the city's best schools.

en: Unusual enough to be noticed and admired; exceptional
hook: REMARKABLE: worth a REMARK.
story: Remarkable. Unusual enough to be noticed and admired; exceptional. Chloe's neighbour sold vegetables at the city market for thirty years, waking before dawn in every season. Alone, she raised four children and sent all four to university. On the day her youngest became a doctor, the whole lane came out to congratulate her, and Chloe cried a little too. Everyone agreed her life was remarkable. The word is simply remark plus able: something remarkable is worth remarking on. So, what word describes an achievement so exceptional that people cannot stop talking about it? ... Remarkable.

gre.s: What makes the novel ____ is not its plot, which is entirely conventional, but its narrator, who speaks in a voice unlike any other in modern fiction.
gre.clue: a voice unlike any other in modern fiction

example: The rescued hawk made a remarkable recovery, flying again only three weeks after the vet set its broken wing.

en: Far away; distant; slight or faint
hook: REMOTE: far away like a REMOTE village, or a remote chance.
story: Remote. Far away and distant; also, slight or faint, as in a remote chance. Tyler's grandparents live on a remote sandbar island in the middle of a great river, reachable only by boat. One stormy evening, Tyler asked the old boatman whether the ferry would still run. The boatman looked at the black sky and the churning water. [sigh] "Only a remote chance, son." Think of a remote control: it works from far away, and a remote chance is just as far from happening. So, what word means far away, or so slight it hardly exists? ... Remote.

gre.s: Although the doctors admitted there was a ____ chance that the experimental treatment would succeed, they warned the family not to raise their hopes.
gre.clue: warned the family not to raise their hopes

example: The odds that the asteroid will strike Earth are remote, but astronomers plan to keep tracking it for the next fifty years.

en: Small or minor (adj.); to insult by ignoring (verb); an insult
hook: GRE trick: SLIGHT as a verb means to snub someone.
story: Slight. As an adjective, small or minor. As a verb, to insult someone by ignoring them; as a noun, the insult itself. At a cousin's wedding by the sea, the host greeted every guest with hugs. When Ava's mother reached the gate, he looked past her and turned to the next guest. She smiled politely, but Ava saw her hands tremble. It was no slight mistake; it was a slight. The trick: to slight someone is to treat them as slight, too small to notice. So, what verb means to insult someone by treating them as not worth noticing? ... Slight.

gre.s: The ambassador was offended by what she regarded as a deliberate ____: she had been seated at the far end of the table, away from every other head of delegation.
gre.clue: seated at the far end of the table, away from every other head of delegation

example: The novelist took it as a slight when her name was left off the festival poster, even though she was its keynote speaker.

en: Based on valid reasoning; in good condition; reliable
hook: GRE trick: SOUND means solid and valid — a sound argument.
story: Sound. Based on valid reasoning; also, in good condition and reliable. When Brian told his parents he wanted to study in Germany, his father frowned. Then Brian laid out his plan: savings for the first year, a partial scholarship, a part-time job already arranged, and a clear career goal. His father read it twice, [chuckle] then nodded. "Your reasoning is sound." Think of the phrase safe and sound: a sound argument is whole and solid, with no cracks in it. So, what word describes reasoning that is solid and reliable? ... Sound.

gre.s: Although the argument's conclusion was surprising, its reasoning was ____, resting on well-established data and careful logic.
gre.clue: resting on well-established data and careful logic

example: The judge found the engineer's analysis sound and ordered the builder to repair the cracked pillars at his own expense.

en: To originate from; to be caused by
hook: STEM FROM: like a plant's STEM growing from its root.
story: Stem from. To come from, or to be caused by. Abby's little sister would never go near the pond behind their village home, even on the hottest days. One evening their mother explained that the fear stemmed from an old accident: at three, the girl had slipped off a boat and been pulled out just in time. Now Abby understood, and she held her sister's hand a little tighter. Picture a plant: its stem grows from hidden roots, just as a problem can stem from a hidden cause. So, what phrase means to originate from something? ... Stem from.

gre.s: Most of the town's current troubles ____ a single decision made decades ago: closing the factory that once employed half its residents.
gre.clue: a single decision made decades ago

example: Many of the river's pollution problems stem from tanneries upstream that dump untreated waste directly into the water.

en: Not to be trusted; of doubtful quality
hook: GRE trick: SUSPECT as an adjective means questionable.
story: Suspect. Not to be trusted; of doubtful quality. A website promised Justin a full scholarship abroad if he paid a five hundred dollar fee within twenty-four hours. The page was full of spelling mistakes, gave no office address, and listed a phone number nobody answered. His professor took one look and said, "This offer is suspect." Justin [gasp] realised how close he had come to paying. Usually a suspect is a person the police doubt; here the word describes anything that deserves the same doubt. So, what word describes an offer or a claim that cannot be trusted? ... Suspect.

gre.s: The study's conclusions are ____, since it was funded by the very company whose product it praises and its raw data have never been released.
gre.clue: funded by the very company whose product it praises

example: Curators considered the painting's signature suspect, since the artist had always signed with his initials and never with his full name.

en: Relating to or done by everyone; applicable in all cases
hook: UNIVERSAL: across the whole UNIVERSE.
story: Universal. Done by or relating to everyone; true in all cases. At the start of each school year, children across the country, in city schools and on river islands alike, receive brand-new free textbooks. Mike still remembers the smell of fresh paper and ink the morning his daughter came home hugging hers. The goal behind it is universal education: every child, with no exceptions. Universal comes from universe, everything that exists, so a universal rule leaves no one out. So, what word describes something that applies to everyone, everywhere? ... Universal.

gre.s: The proposal enjoyed nearly ____ support within the committee: of its forty members, only one voted against it.
gre.clue: only one voted against it

example: Gravity is universal, so the same force that pulls a mango from its branch also keeps the moon circling Earth.

en: Lacking; not good enough
hook: GRE trick: FOUND WANTING means found lacking, not desiring.
story: Wanting. Lacking; not good enough. Andrew spent weeks on his first research paper and handed it in proudly. It came back with one line in red ink: "The analysis is wanting." For a moment he thought his professor simply wanted more of it. [chuckle] Then he understood that his analysis fell short, [sigh] and he opened his laptop again. In older English, want meant lack, as in the saying "for want of a nail, the shoe was lost." So, what word describes work that is lacking, not good enough? ... Wanting.

gre.s: The proposal was praised for its ambition, but on close examination its financial projections were found ____, resting on assumptions that no serious economist would accept.
gre.clue: resting on assumptions that no serious economist would accept

example: Judged against modern safety codes, the old stadium's fire exits are sadly wanting, so the city has closed the upper stands.
